articleTitle: Bandpass implementation of the sigma-delta A-D conversion technique
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: A new design of band-pass sigma-delta A-D converter is presented which can encode the signal at the intermediate frequency and then by digital post processing convert to baseband I and Q. The technique of band-pass sigma-delta conversion is described and a method for designing band-pass A-D converters from existing baseband modulator designs is given with an example to illustrate the theory. Practical results are described with the performance specified in conventional RF circuit terms.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fifth order sigma-delta modulator for audio A/D-converter
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion

articleTitle: Phase-plane analysis of high speed A/D converters with sine waves
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Describes a method of measuring analog-to-digital converter (ADC) errors by applying a sine wave at the input and comparing it to the digitized output data. This permits appropriate corrections to be made to the ADC circuitry. The authors present the details of phase-plane analysis of several state-of-the-art ADCs. They illustrate the power of this technique by presenting an example that reveals imperfections which result in a small step function in the transfer function of the ADC. This technique provides the designers with valuable insight into the cause of the ADC errors which can improve the performance of the devices.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: QMF-based A/D converters: overview and new results
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Provides an overview of A/D converters incorporating a quadrature mirror filter bank. The major difference existing between these and the time-interleaved architectures (both make use of an array of A/D converters) is that, in the former case, suitable bandpass filters are used before and after the quantizers, reducing the effect of quantization noise produced by the array of A/D converters, as shown here. The noise introduced by the switched-capacitor filters, which implement the analysis filter bank in the QMF-based data converters, is estimated. Simulation results obtained with images are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New design techniques yield low power, high resolution delta-sigma and SAR ADCS for process control, medical, seismic and battery-powered applications
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Design innovation using CMOS technology has resulted in an array of new high resolution analog-to-digital converters (ADCs). New design techniques such as on-chip self-calibration have brought about more accurate successive approximation register (SAR) and delta-sigma ADCs. Three ADCs are discussed. These new chips are designed with proven CMOS processes and result in superior performance with very low power dissipation. The three A-to-D converters are: (1) 16-bit four channel DC measurement delta-sigma; (2) 16-bit self-calibrating 25 kHz SAR. (3) 24-bit variable bandwidth delta-sigma converter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On A/D converter linearization using two-dimensional error-correction tables
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Addresses the use of two-dimensional error-correction tables in the linearization of analog-to-digital transfer functions with short memory. The method is applied to the linearization of analog-to-digital (A/D) converters. A/D converter linearity is a key performance limiter in instantaneous wide-bandwidth spectral analysis applications. The authors demonstrate that two-dimensional error-correction tables, generated by a single (i.e. simple) calibration frequency of decreasing amplitude, can reduce harmonic distortion and most intermodulation products in A/D converters over a wide bandwidth relative to the Nyquist bandwidth. Two-dimensional 'phase-plane' and 'state-space' error-correction tables are used to linearize a state-of-the-art 12-bit, 10-megasamples per second (Msps) A/D converter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A/D converter characterization for high-performance signal processing applications
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: This paper presents a state-of-the-art A/D instrumentation facility and the measurement methods used to investigate the effects of A/D converter noise and linearity in two applications-wide-bandwidth spectral analysis and an airborne surveillance radar. These two application-specific examples are used to illustrate the dependence of system requirements on A/D converter specifications. For example, knowing the A/D converter parameters that influence system performance allows the A/D converter designer to trade linearity for noise. To illustrate these trade-offs, the authors show that the key specification for wide-bandwidth spectral signal analysis is high linearity, whereas for an airborne radar application, the A/D converter should be designed for a high dynamic range (DR).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A bandpass Sigma Delta A/D convertor for a digital AM receiver
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Illustrates the design methodology for analogue-to-digital convertors based on bandpass sigma-delta modulation. A digital AM receiver is used as the application to guide the design process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamic testing of analogue to digital converters
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Describes a method for the generation of the transfer characteristic of an analogue to digital converter (ADC) at arbitrary frequency. The technique allows accurate estimation of many important converter parameters from a single test, providing designers with valuable insight into the cause of ADC errors, and is fast in production use. Some comparison are made between the new technique and more conventional methods of test. Requirements for, and example results from the use of the technique are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Broadband high dynamic range A/D conversion limitations
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: The principal objective of this paper is to establish the relationships which exist among the parameters of a digital receiver system which includes, as a minimum, (1) an RF-to-Baseband translator, (2) an A/D Converter, and (3) a digital filter. Certain basic parameters describe the performance of each of these modules in the signal space in which each functions. By placing in evidence several fundamental relationships which exist among these basic parameters, one can provide for the establishment of system performance limitations and can provide a basis for system performance optimizations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A 20-bit sigma-delta D/A converter prototype for audio applications
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Introduces a high resolution sigma-delta D/A converter for audio applications. The digital part of the prototype consist of two in-house full-custom chips implemented using a 2 mu m CMOS technology. The analog part has one commercial chip for the one-bit D/A conversion and standard discrete components for the reconstruction filter. The prototype demonstrates that a good performance can be achieved using simple simple straightforward analog structures. The preliminary measurements indicate over a 100 dB dynamic range.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Matrix analysis of interpolation noise in digital to analogue conversion
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Extends interpolation noise theory, and finds an analytical solution which allows one to relate baseband noise to the switching patterns used. This solution is independent of the type of interpolation scheme. A 'matrix analysis' method is presented in this paper which establishes an analytical relationship between different interpolation schemes. This method has made it possible to devise ways of minimising the baseband interpolation noise.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A vertically structured fast high resolution ADC
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Conceptually the vertical structure is a subranging converter but operates on a different principle which eliminates some of the disadvantages of the classical subranging ADC. Instead of subranging with coarse ADC, DAC, and subtracting amplifier the input voltage is divided into several subranges and a window-amplifier is used for simplification of each subrange.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multibit oversampled DAC with dynamic matching of current sources
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Conventional binary-weighted and oversampling techniques are very popular methods of performing D/A conversions. However, the accuracy required in the component matching limits the resolution obtainable with a binary-weighted converter to approximately 8 bits, unless very sophisticated techniques (including selfcalibration) are used. Moreover, the resolution which can be achieved with an oversampled converter is limited by the oversampling factor actually obtainable for a predetermined signal bandwidth with any given integration technology. This paper presents a novel combined conversion approach, which takes advantage of the positive features of both the above techniques. The most significant bits (MSBs) are converted with the binary-weighted technique, while the least significant bits (LSBs) are converted with the oversampling technique.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A PWM DAC for digital audio power conversion: from theory to performance
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Digital pulse width modulation (PWM) is combined with simple noise shaping to convert 8 times Nyquist sampled digital audio signals directly to analogue audio. A digital interpolating filter is used to provide such over-sampled test signals from a compact disc (CD). A low noise crystal based oscillator is used to synchronise the required digital elements via fast asynchronous counters based on 1.3 mu CMOS. Output is suitable for power-efficient control of MOSFET switching devices and can be used directly, giving >100 dB dynamic range and >120 dB peak signal to noise floor ratio. Comparison between a pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) digital to analogue converter (DAC) and the PWM converter is shown using spectral plots. The PWM unit is shown to follow theoretical analysis very closely.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the performance of an oversampled analog to digital converter with digital requantizer in feedback path
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Conventional delta-sigma converters limit the complexity of the feedback DAC to a precision single bit which in turn leads to the use of a 1-bit ADC in the feedforward path. A spectrally controlled requantization between the output of the multibit ADC and the input to the 1-bit DAC can be performed with an oversampled digital sigma-delta loop in the feedback path of the analog sigma-delta loop. This paper we describes and reports on the hardware implementation of an enhanced performance delta-sigma loop modified to use a multibit ADC in the feedforward path along with a 1-bit DAC in the feedback path.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A comparison of two-stage, 4th-order and single state 2nd-order delta-sigma modulation in digital-to-analogue conversion systems
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Considers the application of delta-sigma modulation (DSM) as a means of digital-to-analogue conversion (DAC) where the aim is to compare conversion structures that can achieve a dynamic range approaching 20 bit (linear PCM resolution) over a 0-20 kHz frequency band. Specifically, a comparison is made between a 2nd-order noise shaped and oversampled 1 bit, DSM converter with a 4th-order multi-level, noise shaped scheme in tandem with an open-loop multi-level to 1 bit mapping converter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling the transfer characteristic of nonideal ADCs exhibiting integral nonlinearity
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Presents a mathematical model for the transfer characteristic of an ADC exhibiting INL. Using this model, closed-form expressions can be obtained for the spectrum of the harmonic distortion resulting from the INL when a single sinusoid is quantised. Another application for this model is to obtain closed-form expressions for the harmonics of the ADC transfer-characteristic itself. These expressions can be used for characterising the ADC by determining the contribution to INL by each bit failure.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High performance signal acquisition systems for sonar applications
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Examines the technology/complexity balance in high performance sonar data acquisition systems and outlines the development of some signal conditioning and A-to-D convertor systems that use sigma-delta convertor techniques, low complexity digital combiners and recursive interpolators. Various realisations of the basic circuits have been developed for a number of particular applications (with bandwidths ranging from a few hundred Hz to in excess of 100 kHz), using mixtures of thick film, surface mount and VLSI ASIC technologies. The paper demonstrates that low cost signal acquisition systems, with wide dynamic range and modest power requirements, can be routinely produced using these techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fully integrated bitstream analogue-to-digital converter for digital audio
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Philips have been pioneers in the implementation of the bitstream conversion technique for high performance digital audio digital-to-analogue (D/A) converters. This paper discusses the principles of bitstream conversion and the development of the first bitstream stereo analogue-to-digital (A/D) converter from Philips. This device consists of a input buffer which can be configured by the user for pre-scaling and anti-aliasing filtering, a third order sigma delta modulator with a performance of better tan 90 dB total harmonic distortion (THD)+noise, and decimation filters with anti-aliasing suppression of greater than 93 dB and inband ripple of less than 0.0002 dB. The device outputs data in a number of selectable formats.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High speed multibit oversampling noise shaping ADCs
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: For very high speed operation, single bit oversamplers have disadvantages when compared to multibit devices. However, achieving the linearity in the feedback DAC has hitherto prevented the widespread adoption of the multibit approach. A new technique is demonstrated that achieves arbitrary linearity, and low noise, from the feedback DAC without the use of calibration. The application to monolithic ADCs, with dynamic ranges in excess of 100 dB at signal bandwidths in excess of 10 MHz, is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Enhancing strictly-digital dither through digital signal processing
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: With the powerful digital signal processing power available today, many traditionally analogue techniques are being re-examined to consider whether processing in the digital domain is preferable. The application of dither is one such technique which has been shown theoretically to benefit from transferring the processing to the digital domain. Strictly-digital dither is more controllable in the sense that it can adapt to the physical converter errors which result in differential linearity and integral linearity errors. This ability is particularly significant if the application is data acquisition (i.e. absolute value, mean, statistics) as opposed to signal acquisition (time history). This paper will show that adding strictly-digital dither is realisable practically and that additional signal processing can further enhance the data acquisition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High speed residue ADCS using differential current-mode techniques
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Current-mode design techniques are readily applicable to data conversion products and promise higher speed, high accuracy ADCs. Combining current-mode and differential design techniques brings even greater benefits-particularly in monolithic designs, where noise immunity and rejection of supply interference is critical. This paper looks at the application of differential, current-mode techniques to the development of fast monolithic residue algorithm ADCs at the 12 bit level and above, with particular reference to two current BiCMOS parts.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Converters operating at one gigahertz
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Look at the advances made in high speed data converter products for speeds approaching 1 GHz. Two key developments in this area are discussed. The first is an 8-bit 450 MHz digital to analogue converter and the progression to a 1 GHz device. The second is a 7-bit 1.0 GSPS analogue to digital converter fabricated on an ultra high speed bipolar process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A wideband complex ADC
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: A wideband complex ADC using baseband digitisation is described. The unambiguous (flat) signal bandwidth is in excess of +or-5 MHz, and the unit operates with IF inputs between 60 and 70 MHz.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Practical design of noise shaper in second-order delta-sigma A/D modulator
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to show the impact of practical design details on noise shaping characteristics and test yields of second-order single-loop Delta-Sigma A/D modulators. Effects of symmetry, of leakages and of crosstalks on quantization noise shaping are analyzed. Techniques used to improve the shaping of quantization noise are discussed. Measurement results from two circuits are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Oversampling data conversion applied to data modulation
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: Oversampling data converters have emerged in recent years as the most feasible solution to high resolution signal conversion. These converters have one major disadvantage over conventional data converters: They require large decimation and/or interpolation filters. Such filters demand significant silicon area and dissipate power. Oversampling data converters are particularly attractive in applications where the digital filtering can be reduced or eliminated. Modulators for data transmission represent such an application. This paper presents a new implementation which uses a combination of direct digital synthesis and oversampled noise shaping. The new solution requires little silicon area has a low power dissipation while being simple to program.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimisation of interpolation noise in digital to analogue conversion
publicationTitle: 1991 International Conference on Analogue to Digital and Digital to Analogue Conversion
abstract: The time-averaging (TAI) interpolation technique allows extra resolution to be added to a digital to analogue converter (DAC) by operating it at higher speeds. The basic technique is illustrated for TAI using a digital interpolator (DI). In contrast with other oversampling methods no feedback is used in this system. This deterministic interpolation approach can overcome many of the problems of the noise shaping (NS) systems, caused by practical limitations of DACs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
